 Advertisement Xavier Becerra talks new wealth tax, fees for drivers, High-Speed Rail changes and other plans for California
 Advertisement Updated: 6:44 PM PDT Oct 28, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Ashley Zavala Political Director Xavier Becerra talks new wealth tax, fees for drivers, High-Speed Rail changes and other plans for California
 Updated: 6:44 PM PDT Oct 28, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Ashley Zavala Political Director Xavier Becerra revealed he's preparing a new tax on the state's richest residents, will seriously consider new fees for drivers and corporations and will likely remove the current CEO of the embattled High-Speed Rail if elected governor of California.
 The Democratic candidate shared the plans and other efforts in an interview with California Politics 360 ahead of Tuesday's election. While Becerra has a list of campaign promises including the declaration of a housing state of emergency and a healthcare expansion, the brief conversation focused on the issues he will likely be confronted with in his first year as governor. 
 Advertisement California voter guide 2026: What to know about the propositions and races on the November ballot Becerra's version of a wealth tax
 Becerra's first major problem if elected: California's budget . 
 Financial experts have warned the state's government is spending more money than it's bringing in, resulting in deep deficits over the next several years. While Becerra is against the billionaire tax proposed in Proposition 40, he said he is eyeing a new possible income tax on the wealthiest people in the state. 
 "If we can prove that you're not paying your fair share, and to me, that's pretty basic. If you're a billionaire and you're paying at a lower tax rate than a firefighter or a teacher or a nurse, you're not paying your fair share," Becerra said. 
 Becerra rebuffed the idea of taxing assets, which he noted is in Prop 40. 
 "Having done tax policy for over 20 years in Congress, you want to make sure it's something that's fair, predictable, and stable," he said. 
 Becerra also took aim at corporate tax breaks, saying, "there's a lot of corporate welfare where we give corporations tax breaks where they don't really need them. And if we can't give Californians good health care, why should we give corporations tax breaks?" 
 Healthcare fee for major companies 
 On healthcare, Becerra addressed a new state law that requires the next governor to come up with a plan to hold corporations accountable for employees relying on the state's insurance for low-income people known as Medi-Cal. The law specifically requires a proposal in writing by April of 2027. 
 When asked if major corporations could expect to pay a healthcare fee, Becerra said, "They can expect something if they are not paying sufficient wages, that their own employees who work full time still qualify for government-subsidized health care under Medi-Cal." 
 "That's not right," Becerra said. "Taxpayers are helping pay for the healthcare for workers because their companies, their employers aren't paid that enough. How do we do it? That's where I have to work with the Legislature to make sure we can do it." 
 He added, "Whether it's a fee, whether it's working the system so that maybe the employers will boost the support, the benefits that they give their workers, one way or the other, people who work full time should not have to ask taxpayers to cover their health care bills."
 A mileage tax 
 While California's gas tax gets a lot of attention, we asked Becerra about a potential mileage tax. 
 With concerns that the state's gas tax may soon be unreliable to fund roads and bridges, California officials are set to complete a report by the end of this year studying the possibility of a tax for drivers based on the number of miles they travel in their vehicle. 
 When asked if, as governor, he would support the new fee, Becerra said "Everything should be on the table." 
 "Our roads aren't maintained just by some magic wand. We have to pay for it. Do I want to tax people more than necessary? No. Should we pay a gas tax? Yes. Should people who drive electric vehicles, who don’t need gas, pay for those roads to be repaired as well? Absolutely."
 High-Speed Rail changes 
 California's embattled project has historically faced cost overruns and delays but has faced new challenges this year with CEO Ian Choudri. Those challenges range from his arrest, a lack of transparency around the project's financial situation, his relationship with a consulting firm associated with the project, and questionable spending the authority approved for project consultants. 
 When asked how he's feeling about the optics around Choudri, Becerra said, "Not good." 
 When asked if Choudri will keep his job under a Gov. Becerra, he signaled that it's not likely. 
 "We’re going to have to scrub a lot. High-speed rail has got to look really different if we’re going to continue this project," Becerra said. "I need the faith of the public in order to make these projects go. I think the public is quickly losing faith if they haven't already in High-Speed Rail."
 "I need to gain the confidence of the public," Becerra said. "I can't gain it if I keep the same characters in place." 
 Paying back California's major COVID-19 debt 
 Becerra committed to addressing the $22 billion debt California owes the federal government for COVID-19 unemployment benefits. California is the only state in the nation that has not paid it back.
 Because the state's government defaulted on the loan, businesses large and small have been shouldering the debt in the form of increased payroll taxes that will grow every year until the debt is paid. 
 "We have to make sure that employers and workers and the state government work together," Becerra said. "I will commit to lower the tab of the debt service, the debt burden that we have."
 The death penalty 
 On the death penalty, Becerra confirmed he would continue Gov. Gavin Newsom's moratorium. "Given what we’ve seen with the death penalty, I’m not interested in enforcing it." 
 When asked if he supports the possibility that Gov. Newsom commutes some or all of the 560 death sentences to life without parole, Becerra said, "I don't know what he's facing, I don't know what the particular cases are."
 "I absolutely, now that he has said he is going to take this on, I wish him every opportunity to make the best call on these cases because these are tough," Becerra said. "I won't weigh in on that cause I don't know what he's looking at." 
 When asked if victims should have to relive those cases through the commutation Becerra said, "That’s where talking to the families, the victims’ families is going to be really important because you want to make sure that they understand what we’re doing. I think we want to be humane." 
 Wildfire liability 
 An ongoing fight at the state capitol is whether to limit how much investor-owned utility companies like PG&E and Southern California Edison pay when they cause a catastrophic fire. The companies this year pushed to end or limit the right of insurance companies to sue them to recoup their losses. 
 When asked if he would be willing to limit that right of insurance companies, Becerra committed to working on the issue, but did not provide specifics, acknowledging state lawmakers and Gov. Newsom are still trying to address the concerns. 
 "I don’t have all the details that tI do know this, that we can’t go on with wildfires this way, where the folks who suffer the most are the very victims who lose their homes," Becerra said. 
 Capitol Annex transparency 
 If elected, Becerra would be the first governor to move into the new, controversial Capitol Annex at the end of 2027. The project is costing state taxpayers at least $1.2 billion and project leaders refuse to give up key cost-related records until the project is finished. 
 When asked if he'll open up the books on the project, Becerra said, "I want us to be as transparent as possible."
 "I suspect I’ve heard that some of the problems of being overly transparent are security issues that would put certain information in harm’s way. So I don’t know what the reason for all the confidentiality, but I believe in transparency. And when I was A.G., I enforced transparency," Becerra said. 
 When asked if it's fair to keep records from the public the way project leaders have been Becerra said, "I don't know what the grounds are for delaying." 
 "There are very few reasons for us to tell the public they don't have access to their own records."
 Biggest difference between Becerra and Newsom
 When asked about the biggest difference between him and California's current Democratic Gov. Newsom, Becerra first replied in Spanish, noting, his fluency in Spanish is one of the various ways he would be different. He pointed to his background, his immigrant parents. 
 "I am my own person and with the support of voters, I hope to be able to show them that we’ll get stuff done," he said. 
 Newsom has been known to challenge state lawmakers by trying to bypass the typical legislative process on major issues by passing new laws through the state's fast-paced state budget process. 
 When asked if Becerra would do the same, he said he has already told lawmakers he intends to go to them early with proposals. 
 "I got a big cheer for that," Becerra said, smiling. 
 He also said he's hoping he can reduce the number of bills that go through the Legislature, which previous governors like Newsom and Jerry Brown have criticized .
